newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: In war of symbols, S.Korean unions are victorious.
newsitem.headline: In war of symbols, S.Korean unions are victorious.

text.p: Joining a statue of the Virgin Mary, a figure of Christ the Redeemer and a nativity grotto on the grounds of Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral is another vivid symbol -- a trade unionists' tent.
Clergy and choristers hurry past shaven-headed union leaders camped in the makeshift strike headquarters on their way to morning prayers.'
And riot police besieging the gothic church outnumber worshippers.

Small wonder South Korea's government is having trouble winning a public relations battle with the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions that has led bitter strikes against a contested labour law that allows worker layoffs, replacement of strikers and flexible working hours.
Its latest gambit -- a challenge to strike leaders on Saturday for a televised debate -- was contemptuously dismissed as a propaganda ploy.
Many South Koreans acknowledge that reform of their labour laws is long overdue.
A jobs-for-life tradition was fine while the economy was growing in double digits, but in these days of contraction it has become a liability.
Likewise, flexible shifts are a must for struggling electronics makers anxious to keep inventories low and respond to "just-in-time" consumer demand.
Yet while economic commentators argue that many provisions of the new law make sense, the government seems to have botched its case.

It failed to balance free-market provisions demanded by employers with a key concession demanded by the current strike leaders for freedom of association for workers. The confederation remains outlawed: the normally docile Federation of Korean Trade Unions retains the union monopoly it was granted by past authoritarian governments.
And the government's heavy-handedness in ramming through the law, and then threatening strike leaders with arrest, has aroused public sympathy for the workers' cause.
The New Korea Party adopted the law in a clandestine six-minute session of parliament held at dawn while opposition deputies slept.
It attached the bill to a law reviving the powers of a domestic spy agency once notorious for torturing and kidnapping political dissidents.
In the eyes of many Koreans, such methods hark back to the days of military repression when labour leaders were routinely tossed in jail.

Now the rights and wrongs of the labour law have been obscured in a battle of symbols played out on the snow-covered grounds of Seoul's Roman Catholic cathedral, where strike leaders are resisting arrest.
The longer the stand-off continues the less likely a violent end to the strikes becomes. International media have descended on Myongdong in recent days.

Pressures are mounting on President Kim Young-sam to compromise, not least from South Korea's new partners in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, who have reminded Seoul of its obligations to respect human rights and freedom of association under the terms of its entry to the Paris-based club in December.
Kim has described the furore over the law as a "big misunderstanding".
But a greater error of reckoning may have been the government's failure to predict the depth of domestic and international opposition, and the staying power of the strikers.
Almost three weeks after strikes began the day after Christmas, workers are still livid. Unions have called for the biggest strike in South Korea's history this week.
